sections.content: Boids Simulation was an experimental project that I took on to challenge my understanding of optimization. I first gained exposure to the concept of group motion and flocking behavior modeling in college, and I was fascinated by the complexity involved to mimic the simple graces found in the natural world. Through this project, I was able to develop increasingly efficient boids simulations, ultimately creating a model that could run at a much higher FPS rate (for example, 400 birds visualized at 70 FPS with the naive model vs 400 birds at 700 FPS with my optimized one, i.e. a 10 fold difference).

items: Engine: Unity
Programming Languages: C#, HLSL
- Spatial partitioning for neighbor search
- Compute shader implementation
- Time complexity and performance optimization
- I developed 5 separate levels of flock modeling with increasing optimization
- I learned how to write a compute shader.
- I created front-end UI components to make the model more user-friendly and adaptable in real time.

Boids are artificial bird-like or bird-oid objects originally modeled by Craig Reynolds in order to simulate the flocking patterns of birds and group motion. This artificial life simulation relies on 3 simple rules:
- Separation: Strength of force to stay away from other boids
- Alignment: Strength of force to look in the same direction as other boids
- Cohesion: Strength of force to stay close to other boids
My boid simulator is fundamentally built on these same concepts and adheres to these 3 rules.
My goal was to establish 5 different simulation modes with various levels of optimization.
Model 1: Naive Boids
- It applies the 3 boid rules independently.
- For each rule, each boid performs a check against all other boids in the simulation resulting in 3 O(n^2) passes per frame
- Incredibly inefficient and scales exponentially worse as more boids are added to the simulation
Model 2: Single Pass Evaluation
- Combines the separation, alignment, and cohesion into a single iteration
- Instead of scanning all boids 3 times, it scans all boids once and applies all 3 rules simultaneously
- It is still a O(n^2) time complexity but it has lower cost because it is done once instead of 3 times
Model 3: Spatial Partition Neighbor Search
- Instead of searching for every boid in the simulation, it first divides space into grids
- Boids are then keep track of the partition that it is in and only needs to check neighboring grid partitions for neighboring boids
- Fastly reduces the average number of neighboring comparisons. It still has a O(n^2) time complexity at worse when the partitions are too large, but on average has a much lower one
- In this implementation it applies the 3 boid rules independently
Model 4: Spatial Partition Single Pass
- Exact same as the 3rd implementation but has the 2nd implementation of a single pass
Model 5: Compute Shader Implementation
- Implemented the 2nd optimized naive algorithm by running it on the GPU in parallel via a compute shader
- This shifts the workload from the CPU to the GPU which is a more optimized hardware for large simultaneous processing
Once the models were complete, I wanted to update the UI to allow the simulator to make real-time adjustments without restarting the entire simulation.
- I included parameters that allowed real time controls for the boid count, rule weights, perception radii, speed limits, turn rate, and drag
- I created an on-screen FPS counter to provide immediate feedback onto the effectiveness of the various levels of optimization
- I furthermore integrated a toggleable option which changes the color of boids in relation to their maximum speed for more visual clarity and feedback
Overall, being able to adjust the aforementioned values in made it effective and entertaining to experiment with these models.

sections.content: This game, titled “Overtime Deliveries,” was created in a joint effort between myself and my friend Kevin. I was responsible for the following: octree implementation, drone controls, package retrieval system, package deployment system, explosion animations, and drone modeling. Meanwhile, Kevin was responsible for modeling the terrain and lighting effects. Together, we were able to expand upon an assignment that only called for a “lunar landing simulator” and created a playable and fun game in which the player controls a drone and must pick up packages and deliver them to spots on the map, ensuring that the packages do not break on release. This was a blast to create with my friend and taught me how to optimize complex terrain collision detection via Octrees. I got a lot of joy out of directly visualizing the algorithm and implementing it in an interactive way.

items: Engine: N/A
Coding Language: C++
- Optimized complex terrain collision detection via Octrees
- Implemented physics based movement controller
- I collaborated effectively on different parts with a partner
- We completed this project in only 1 week
The following is a summary of the components I worked on in this project:

- An octree is a tree-data structure in which each internal node has exactly eight children made to take in vertex/mesh data of a terrain model and divide up space of the complex model to create a series of hitboxes to describe the shape of the space. This allows for quick search at a point by moving through the octree

- I chose to use the octree because despite initial slowing for an initial creation of the octree, this system vastly makes up for speed of determining points of contact between objects and the mesh during real movements
- I created a physics-based flight simulation

- I programmed a system in which pressing on the various arrow keys caused a force to be applied in the corresponding direction adjusted for the direction that the drone was facing (example: if facing south direction, the up arrow will move south, right will move west, etc)
- I also accounted for force in the vertical movement of the drone

- Most importantly, I ensured that when colliding with the octree/terrain, the terrain calculated the appropriate normal value on average based on the collisions being detected and pushed the drone back away from the terrain
- We wanted to have a fun game system in which the user had the ability pick up packages and release them
- Once released, packages were programmed to fall according to gravity, eventually colliding with the ground
- In order to add challenge to the game, I made it so that depending on the speed of the package at the time of ground-strike, a package could be destroyed
- I added a particle system which created an explosion of particles whenever the package collided with the floor. This created visual allure and drama in the game.
- Modeled the drone myself entirely in Maya. I was inspired by science fiction stories with dystopian drone delivery systems that reign beyond the existence of humanity itself.

sections.content: As the name might suggest, Ringsweeper is inspired by Minesweeper, one of my favorite games of all time (please don’t judge my record time of 74 seconds on expert mode). When my friend Tuukka and I decided to join the 2025 Game Maker’s Took Kit (GMTK) Game Jam, I knew that we wanted to explore Unity’s shader graph and explore the VFX graph, so we decided to create a 3D version of Minesweeper complete with wave-like effects upon tile reveals and explosions vs fireworks depending on the success of the player. I enjoyed the challenge of working under the time crunch of a game jam while getting to explore this new skillset with one of my closest friends.

items: Engine: Unity
Coding Language: C#
- Recursive implementation of reveal
- Procedurally orient objects onto spline path
- Designed and completed the game in only 4 days
- I learned how to create visual effects using Unity’s shader graph and VFX graph

sections.content: In order to explain Ringsweeper, it is important to talk about the inspiration behind it:

Minesweeper. Minesweeper is a logic puzzle game centered around a board with hidden mines dispersed throughout a board of clickable tiles. The goal of the game is to clear the board without detonating any mines.

items: For our project, our first step was to break down the rules of Minesweeper and implement them into Ringsweeper. Here is a breakdown of Minesweeper:
- The game is set on a grid
- The first click of the game won’t be a mine but instead an empty tile
- After the first click, the game generates the board by placing all of the mines randomly across the grid
- If the player presses onto a mine, all mines are revealed and the game is over
- Mine tiles once revealed provide information on the number of mines in the 3x3 grid surrounding that tile
- Using the information provided, the player can mark unrevealed tiles as mines to ensure they remember where they are and to not select a mine accidentally
- The information provided by the tiles and the assumption of where known mine tiles are, the player can then label safe tiles
- The game ends once the player as revealed all non-bomb tiles inside of the entire grid

sections.content: For our purposes, we implemented similar mine logic with random placement of mines across a grid shaped like a ring. We made sure that each tile kept track of adjacent mines.

Ringsweeper was designed to be more than just a 3D copy of Minesweeper though. We had a number of new elements that we wanted to add and that came with creating a ring-like system rather than a flat grid.

items: Recursive based implementation of the revealing of tiles

- We wanted to make revealing of tiles more satisfying, so we made it so that when a user presses an empty tile, it reveals the connected tiles sequentially (this is in contrast to traditional Minesweeper where all tiles are revealed simultaneously).
- This implementation took in the direction that the wave is approaching from in order to rotate tiles in the appropriate/corresponding direction.

- I chose a recursive implementation because in this circumstance, I realized that there is no consistent iterative length to the expanding wave meaning that instead the function must continually call itself to reveal more tiles as new tiles are being revealed by the wave.
Wrapping Rule Adjustment

- Since the Ringsweeper map is in the shape of a cylinder, the ends of the game wrap and connect. Unlike Minesweeper where the ends on either side do not interact with each other at all, we now had to implement a continuous system.
- I programmed the game so that when a mine is randomly placed onto the ends of the grid, they must affect the mine count of the non-mine tiles on the other end.
Spline Implementation
- A spline is a piecewise parametric curve used to approximate shapes through curves
- Since we wanted to make the game in the shape of a cylinder, a spline was the perfect method to create the visual we wanted.
- I therefore created a function that mapped the grid onto a spline. This ultimately gave me, as well as any other designer/developer, full control to shape and build the grid in any 3D path
Unique Visual Effects
- There were a number of visual elements that we wanted to create to make the game visually appealing:
- Skybox: a method of creating backgrounds to make video game levels appear large
-- I created a custom skybox inside of Unity’s shader graph designed to look like purple galaxies so that the players felt immersed in space
- Stopwatch:

-- I designed a stopwatch with segmented displays for each of the digits. This vintage feel paid homage to the original Minesweeper while functionally counting the time that the player has spent trying to solve the Ringsweeper grid
- Loss effects:

-- I wanted to make loss effects reveal how I felt after losing a game of Minesweeper, so for Ringsweeper I spent a lot of time making a custom loss effect where all the bombs revealed themselves then a dramatic explosion burst from the center of the cylinder
- Win animations:

-- Similarly, I wanted a visual effect that captured the joy of a successful game so I created a win animation with fireworks emerging from the central stopwatch. This was done using Unity’s VFX graph.

sections.content: A Life Well Lived is a narrative-driven, choose-your-own-adventure game developed during a game jam. My primary contribution was the creation of a custom dialogue tooling system that allowed a team of writers to author and connect branching narrative content efficiently.
The project emphasized iteration speed and close collaboration between technical and non-technical team members.

I designed a dialogue graph system where narrative nodes could be authored and connected through a structured interface. This allowed writers to build branching dialogue without requiring programmer intervention.
The system was fully data-driven, enabling rapid iteration and easy modification of narrative structure throughout development.
Special attention was given to preventing broken narrative paths by validating connections and identifying incomplete nodes early. This reduced runtime errors and made iteration safer during the jam.
The runtime system cleanly traverses dialogue states, ensuring consistent behavior regardless of narrative complexity.

items: Designing tools for usability rather than raw flexibility
Supporting non-technical collaborators through good editor UX
The importance of validation in data-driven narrative systems
How tooling directly impacts team velocity

sections.content: Truckbomb is an in-development, chaotic, endless arcade driving game focused on multitasking under pressure. The player must drive while simultaneously managing multiple escalating minigames that demand constant attention.
This was a longer-term collaborative project developed with a group of designers and developers.
Given the chaotic nature of the game, my work focused on ensuring that information was communicated clearly and instantly, even as multiple systems competed for the player’s attention.
UI elements and visual effects were designed to reinforce urgency while remaining readable under pressure.
I contributed to feature implementation, UI elements, and VFX across multiple minigames, including engine repair, wheel maintenance, radio tuning, and bomb defusal.
Each minigame required a distinct visual language while still fitting cohesively within the overall aesthetic of the game.
Working on a longer-term project required adapting to an evolving codebase and continuously iterating based on playtesting and team feedback.

items: Designing systems that communicate instantly under cognitive load
Balancing chaos with readability through UI and VFX
Collaborating effectively within an evolving team project
Iterative refinement based on real player behavior
